extracted.intended_audience: playwrights and literate public interested in theatre, manners, and moral instruction (early-18th-century readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for composing and judging stage plays and comic works that influence manners and public morals—what subjects, characterizations, and dramatic effects are appropriate or inappropriate. Emphasis on avoiding lewdness, selecting proper subjects for ridicule, and ensuring vice is not glamorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage should promote virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: "Were our English Stage but half so virtuous as that of the Greeks or Romans, we should quickly see the Influence of it in the Behaviour of all the Politer Part of Mankind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theatre ought to recommend religion, government, and public worship; it should shape manners so that ridicule of religion, the man of pleasure being the model gentleman, or the triumph of vanity would not be fashionable. Plays should influence audiences toward better behaviour rather than encourage vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plays ought to be subject to inspections and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: "If the English Stage were under the same Regulations the Athenian was formerly, it would have the same Effect... Were our Plays subject to proper Inspections and Limitations, we might not only pass away several of our vacant Hours in the highest Entertainments; but should always rise from them wiser and better than we sat down to them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic performances should be regulated so they entertain without corrupting; censorship/inspection is proposed as a means to ensure the stage contributes to moral improvement and leaves the audience wiser and better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict theatrical licentiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is one of the most unaccountable things in our Age, that the Lewdness of our Theatre should be so much complained of, so well exposed, and so little redressed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active effort should be made to restrain licentiousness on stage because current abuses exclude multitudes (e.g., fathers fearing their daughters will be ruined); theatre should assist the advancement of morality and reformation of the age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray vices so they are not laudable
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whatever Vices are represented upon the Stage, they ought to be so marked and branded by the Poet, as not to appear either laudable or amiable in the Person who is tainted with them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When vices appear in characters, the dramatist must ensure the representation condemns them (branding/shaming), rather than making the vice attractive; the audience should not be invited to admire or sympathize with vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never choose an improper subject for ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: "There was another Rule likewise, which was observed by Authors of Antiquity... never to chuse an improper Subject for Ridicule. Now a Subject is improper for Ridicule, if it is apt to stir up Horrour and Commiseration rather than Laughter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects that naturally evoke horror or pity (e.g., incest, murder, violations of the marriage-bed) are inappropriate for comedy; such material properly belongs to tragedy and should not be treated as comic fodder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making cuckoldry the basis of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Cuckoldom is the Basis of most of our Modern Plays. If an Alderman appears upon the Stage, you may be sure it is in order to be Cuckolded."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of the contemporary habit of centering plot and humour around cuckoldry and the humiliating of particular social types; playwrights should avoid relying on such recurring, degrading motifs as cheap comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make immoral characters the favourites of the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "At the same time the Poet so contrives Matters, that the two Criminals are the Favourites of the Audience... The Truth of it is, the accomplished Gentleman upon the English Stage, is the Person that is familiar with other Men's Wives..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatists should avoid structuring plots so that immoral characters are sympathized with or cheered; the audience's emotional alignment should not reward or admire the corrupt behaviour of central figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stereotyped 'fine' people as morally corrupt
rubrics_metrics.description: "I do not know whether it proceeds from Barrenness of Invention... but I have often wondered that our ordinary Poets cannot frame to themselves the Idea of a Fine Man who is not a Whore-master, or of a Fine Woman that is not a Jilt."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should invent refined, admirable characters whose 'fine' qualities are compatible with virtue; do not default to equating gallantry or elegance with sexual immorality or faithlessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedies should leave audiences wiser and better
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays should be such that "we might not only pass away several of our vacant Hours in the highest Entertainments; but should always rise from them wiser and better than we sat down to them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entertainment value should be combined with moral or intellectual improvement; the best dramatic entertainments elevate the audience rather than merely amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray virtuous female character (model of Fidelia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of Fidelia: the only child who devotes youth to caring for a decrepit father; accomplished (reads, dances, sings, plays spinet and lute) but makes filial duty her business and glory, refuses courtship while her father lives, balances accomplishments with devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing female characters of virtue, emphasize filial piety, domestic devotion, refinement of manners, restraint in public gallantry, and the voluntary sacrifice of personal amusements for duty; virtue may coexist with accomplishments and social grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict the moral consequences of trivial falsehoods and broken promises
rubrics_metrics.description: Essay on neglect of promises and light infidelity: small failures to keep appointments and trivial falsities lead to loss of trust and deteriorating integrity ("The first Steps towards Ill are very carefully to be avoided...").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small social breaches (broken promises, habitual lateness, trivial lies) in characterization and plot to show the erosion of honesty and reputation; treat minor moral failings as indicators of larger corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use habit/custom as a moral development mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: From reflection that 'Custom is a second Nature' and 'Optimum vitæ genus eligito, nam consuetudo faciet jucundissimum' (choose the best life; custom will make it delightful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In narrative or character arcs, show how repeated practice and custom can turn difficult or initially disagreeable virtuous actions into pleasures and stable character traits; habit is a plausible engine for moral change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray effects of money on character and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that money governs many actions and can 'bring the Politician, the Merchant, and the Lawyer' and that money has 'great Supports they afford us under the severest Calamities' and may influence honesty and piety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting wealth, show both its temptations (corroding honesty) and its stabilizing effects (providing security, supporting piety); use money as a complex motivator rather than a one-dimensional vice.
